### Geometric formulation

Geometrically a gauge theory is described in terms of a principal bundle with the gauge group as its fiber, and the gauge field is a connection on this principal bundle. [TODO]

### Local formulation

Despite the geometric formulation being global, in practice gauge theories are often described locally. This local formulation is what is commonly used in physics, particularly in the context of electromagnetism and the Standard Model. Here one is much less reliant on certain choices one
has to make regarding for example the regularity of the fields associated with the principal bundle.

We first introduce a general concept called *local gauge data*, which abstractly encapsulates
all the information needed to describe gauge transformations and gauge fields at a
single spacetime point.

#### Local gauge data

If one only cares about local gauge transformations, one can ask what data is needed at a point x.
Let G be the gauge group and 𝔤 its Lie algebra. A local Lagrangian sees a gauge transformation only
through its action on the fields and finitely many of their derivatives at x, and so only through
the Taylor series of the gauge transformation at x. If every smooth function is an allowed gauge
transformation, Borel's theorem shows that every Taylor series compatible with G arises, convergent
or not. These Taylor series, the jets at x, form a group G_J, and their infinitesimal counterparts a
Lie algebra 𝔤_J over ℝ.

So at x, a gauge transformation is replaced by its jet U ∈ G_J, and an infinitesimal gauge
transformation by a jet a ∈ 𝔤_J. The data needed at x is whatever enters the transformation laws. A
gauge field A_μ is Lie algebra valued, and under U it transforms as A_μ ↦ Ad_U A_μ + θ_μ(U). Here
Ad_U is the adjoint action, U A_μ U⁻¹ for a matrix group, and θ_μ(U) = i (∂_μ U) U⁻¹ is the
Maurer–Cartan form, the inhomogeneous term that makes A_μ a gauge field rather than a matter field.
A Lagrangian also involves derivatives of the gauge field, as in the field strength
F_μν = ∂_μ A_ν − ∂_ν A_μ + ⁅A_μ, A_ν⁆ with ⁅A, B⁆ = i (AB − BA), so one needs the spacetime
derivatives ∂_μ of Lie algebra jets, together with multiplication by a coordinate x_μ to build jets
with prescribed derivatives. Finally, a jet can be evaluated at x, giving U(x) ∈ G and a(x) ∈ 𝔤, and
a global gauge transformation g ∈ G, or c ∈ 𝔤, gives a constant jet. We define *local gauge data* to
be exactly this information: G, 𝔤, G_J, 𝔤_J and these operations, subject to the rules that make the
transformation laws consistent. Among them are the Leibniz rules
∂_μ ⁅a, b⁆ = ⁅∂_μ a, b⁆ + ⁅a, ∂_μ b⁆ and ∂_μ (x_ν a) = x_ν ∂_μ a + δ_μν a; the cocycle law
θ_μ(UV) = θ_μ(U) + Ad_U θ_μ(V), which says that transforming A_μ by V and then by U is the same as
transforming by UV; and ∂_μ θ_ν(U) − ∂_ν θ_μ(U) + ⁅θ_μ(U), θ_ν(U)⁆ = 0, which says that a pure-gauge
field has vanishing field strength. [9]

Every g ∈ G is the value at x of its constant jet, so evaluation G_J → G is surjective and the
inclusion of constants G → G_J is injective; the same holds for 𝔤_J → 𝔤 and 𝔤 → 𝔤_J. [10] Applied to
constant jets, the rules for G_J and 𝔤_J show that Ad_g is a Lie algebra automorphism of 𝔤 for every
g ∈ G, and that ∂_μ commutes with Ad_g. [11]

For a multiset s of directions, the iterated derivative ∂_s applies ∂_μ once for each μ in s. It
satisfies ∂_(s + t) = ∂_s ∂_t and the iterated Leibniz rule ∂_s ⁅a, b⁆ = Σ ⁅∂_s₁ a, ∂_s₂ b⁆, the sum
running over the ways of splitting s as s₁ + s₂. If s is non-empty then ∂_s c = 0 for every constant
c ∈ 𝔤, and ∂_s commutes with Ad_g for g ∈ G. [12] The value (∂_s (x_μ a))(x) is the number of times
μ occurs in s, multiplied by (∂_(s − μ) a)(x). [13]

A morphism of local gauge data consists of maps G → G', 𝔤 → 𝔤', G_J → G'_J and 𝔤_J → 𝔤'_J compatible
with all of the operations above. It intertwines Ad on 𝔤 and 𝔤', and commutes with ∂_s. [14]
Morphisms have identities and compose. [15] A homomorphism of Lie groups induces a morphism of local
gauge data. [TODO]

#### The abelian theory

In electromagnetism the gauge field is the electromagnetic potential {1}, a Lorentz-vector-valued
field on spacetime, and its field strength is built from that potential. [2][3] A gauge
transformation shifts the potential by the gradient of a scalar {2}, and the pure-gauge potential is
the shift of zero. [4] Gauge transformations leave the field strength invariant. [5] In particular a
pure-gauge potential has vanishing field strength, and this relies on raising the index of the
gradient with the Minkowski metric: the bare gradient of a scalar can have nonzero field
strength. [6] Gauge transformations compose: the trivial shift is the identity and successive shifts
add. [7] They commute with the action of the Lorentz group. [8]

#### The Standard Model gauge group

The Standard Model gauge group {3} is SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1), with its projections onto the three
factors and a central discrete subgroup of sixth roots of unity. [1]

#### The non-abelian theory

A general gauge theory {4} admits an arbitrary Lie group as its structure group. [TODO] Its gauge
field takes values in the Lie algebra of that group. [TODO] Matter fields carry a gauge-covariant
derivative with a definite transformation law. [TODO] The gauge field has a Yang–Mills
curvature. [TODO] That curvature transforms covariantly under gauge transformations. [TODO]
The Yang–Mills action yields the Yang–Mills field equations. [TODO] A gauge field determines
parallel transport along paths and holonomy around loops. [TODO] Gauge fields are connections on
principal bundles. [TODO] Progress on this API is tracked in a GitHub issue {5}.

content.text:
A damped harmonic oscillator {1}{2} is specified by its mass, its spring constant and its damping
coefficient. [1] Its equation of motion, for a trajectory from time {3} into one-dimensional
Euclidean space, is m ẍ + γ ẋ + k x = 0. [2] The force on the mass is −k x − γ ẋ, and the equation
of motion is Newton's second law for that force. [3] With no damping the system is the undamped
harmonic oscillator, and the two equations of motion agree. [6]

The kinetic energy is ½ m ‖ẋ‖², that of the underlying undamped oscillator. [10] The potential
energy is ½ k ‖x‖². [11] Along a solution the mechanical energy dissipates at the rate −γ ‖ẋ‖², and
strictly decreases whenever the velocity is nonzero and the damping is positive. [4]

The discriminant γ² − 4 m k classifies the motion: it is underdamped when the discriminant is
negative, critically damped when it vanishes, and overdamped when it is positive, and each regime
has a decay rate γ/(2m) and an angular frequency. [5] The initial conditions of the oscillator are
an initial position and an initial velocity. [7] The trajectory with those initial conditions has a
closed form appropriate to the damping regime — trigonometric, polynomial or hyperbolic, each
multiplied by an exponential decay. [8] That trajectory satisfies the equation of motion. [9] It is
the unique solution of the equation of motion with the given initial conditions. [14]

The Caldirola–Kanai Lagrangian is the undamped Lagrangian multiplied by the growing exponential
exp(γ t / m). [12] Its variational gradient reduces to the Euler–Lagrange equations, and vanishes
exactly on solutions of the equation of motion. [13] This Lagrangian goes back to Caldirola {4} and
Kanai {5}.

### Phase space and observables

A configuration space Q is a smooth manifold without boundary {1}. [1] For finite-dimensional Q,
its canonical Hamiltonian phase space is the cotangent bundle T*Q: a state consists of a
configuration q and a momentum covector at q. [TODO] This space carries a canonical symplectic form,
independently of the choice of Hamiltonian {6}. [TODO] In the coordinate formulation on a complete
real inner-product space X, states are pairs (p, q) in X × X, and observables are real-valued
functions f(p, q), with momentum first. [2] Identifying the cotangent phase space of a Euclidean
configuration space with this coordinate representation uses the inner product to represent
covectors as momentum vectors. [TODO]

### Hamiltonians and Hamiltonian trajectories

A Hamiltonian system consists of a phase space and a smooth real-valued Hamiltonian, possibly
time-dependent and defined on an open domain. [TODO] The phase space describes kinematics; choosing the
Hamiltonian specifies dynamics through the symplectic form {2}{6}. [TODO] In coordinates, curves
p(t) and q(t) satisfy Hamilton's equations q̇ = ∇ₚH and ṗ = −∇qH exactly when the Hamilton
equation operator vanishes. [3] The symplectic definition of Hamiltonian trajectories agrees with
these coordinate equations. [TODO] For a smooth Hamiltonian and a smooth phase-space curve, the
variational gradient of the action ∫ (⟨p, q̇⟩ − H(t, p, q)) dt is that operator. [4]

For a finite-dimensional real normed configuration space E, an open domain U in E* × E and a
smooth Hamiltonian H on Time × U determine a Hamiltonian system on U with the canonical symplectic
form; E* denotes the continuous dual, containing the momenta {6}. [TODO]

Taking E = ℝ, positive mass m and spring constant k gives the harmonic-oscillator Hamiltonian
H(p, q) = p²/(2m) + k q²/2, which is smooth on the whole phase space. [12] Taking E = ℝ³, positive
mass m and a radial potential V smooth at positive radii gives the central-force Hamiltonian
H(p, q) = ‖p‖²/(2m) + V(‖q‖), smooth on the open domain U = {(p, q) | q ≠ 0}. [14] Using the
Euclidean inner product to identify momenta with vectors, both are Hamiltonian systems obtained
by the preceding construction. [TODO]

The Legendre map sends a velocity v to its conjugate momentum p = ∂L/∂v. If this map has a smooth
inverse over time and configuration space, the Hamiltonian H(t, p, q) = p(v) − L(t, q, v), with
v recovered from (t, p, q), gives the equivalent Hamiltonian description of a Lagrangian system
{5}{6}. [TODO]

### Poisson brackets and observable evolution

The coordinate Poisson bracket is {f, g} = ⟨∇qf, ∇ₚg⟩ − ⟨∇ₚf, ∇qg⟩. [2] It is antisymmetric,
bilinear and satisfies the Leibniz rule, with the differentiability assumptions needed for the
gradient rules. [5] Along a differentiable solution of Hamilton's equations, a time-independent
observable differentiable at the current state satisfies d f(p(t), q(t))/dt = {f, H(t)}(p(t), q(t)).
[6] The canonical coordinate relations are {qᵢ, pⱼ} = δᵢⱼ, {qᵢ, qⱼ} = {pᵢ, pⱼ} = 0, and smooth
observables satisfy the Jacobi identity. [TODO]

### Symmetries and conserved quantities

For a time-independent differentiable observable along a differentiable Hamiltonian trajectory,
a vanishing Poisson bracket with the Hamiltonian implies zero time derivative. [6] A smooth
autonomous Hamiltonian Poisson-commutes with itself and has zero time derivative along its
Hamiltonian trajectories. [5][6] These quantities are constant on connected time intervals,
giving energy conservation in the autonomous case. [TODO]

On a finite-dimensional real symplectic vector space, an affine infinitesimally symplectic Lie
algebra action has a moment map whose components generate the action's vector fields through
their symplectic gradients. [7] If an autonomous Hamiltonian is invariant under a generator, the
corresponding moment-map component is constant along its Hamiltonian trajectories. [8]

### Integrability

For an autonomous Hamiltonian on a 2d-dimensional Euclidean phase space, Liouville integrability
on an open dense domain U consists of d smooth observables, including the Hamiltonian, that
pairwise Poisson-commute and whose phase-space gradients are linearly independent on U. [9] Each
has zero time derivative along a differentiable Hamiltonian trajectory at times when the state
lies in U. [10] With one degree of freedom, the Hamiltonian alone gives integrability on any open
dense domain where it is smooth and its phase-space gradient is nonzero. [11] The Liouville–Arnold
theorem identifies compact connected regular common level sets as invariant tori and supplies
local action–angle coordinates {6}. [TODO]

### Existing examples and their connections

The harmonic oscillator {3} and simple pendulum {4} have explicit canonical momenta and
Hamiltonians, with Hamiltonian, Newtonian and variational descriptions agreeing for smooth
trajectories. The pendulum is expressed using a real lift of its angle. [12][13]

Three-dimensional central-force systems have Hamiltonians smooth away from the centre. [14]
Their angular-momentum observables L² and Lz Poisson-commute with each other and with the
Hamiltonian away from the centre. [15] Their functional independence on a suitable open dense
domain gives central-force Liouville integrability. [TODO]

A point particle of positive mass m in a Euclidean configuration space with a smooth potential V
has Lagrangian L(q, v) = m ‖v‖²/2 − V(q) and Hamiltonian H(p, q) = ‖p‖²/(2m) + V(q), linked by
the momentum p = m v. [TODO]

content.text:
### The configuration space

The configuration space of the classical harmonic oscillator, in the geometric setting of Terek {1},
carries a single global coordinate valued in one-dimensional Euclidean space; two configurations are
equal when their coordinates are, and a configuration can be applied like a function to read off its
coordinate. [1] The configuration space carries the topology induced by its global coordinate, and
is equivalent and homeomorphic to the Euclidean model, which transports Hausdorffness and second
countability across. [2]

The configuration space is a smooth manifold, charted by a single global chart, and that chart is an
analytic diffeomorphism onto the Euclidean model. [3] Each tangent space is a finite-dimensional
normed real vector space, with a chart-induced continuous linear equivalence to the Euclidean
coordinate model. [4] The configuration space maps to the actual position of the particle in
physical space {2}, by reading off the underlying coordinate. [5]

### Trajectories and kinetic energy

A trajectory of the oscillator is a curve from time {3} into the configuration space, with its
coordinate curve and its curve of positions in physical space. [6] A trajectory is smooth exactly
when its coordinate curve is, and likewise differentiable; the geometric velocity is a tangent
vector, and it is the time derivative of the coordinate curve. [7]

The configuration space carries the oscillator's mass Riemannian metric, the mass-scaled Euclidean
inner product in global tangent coordinates, which is positive definite and computable in
coordinates. [8] The geometric kinetic energy of a tangent vector v is ½ g(v, v) for that metric g,
and recovers the standard mass-scaled coordinate expression ½ m ‖v‖². [9]

### Lagrangian systems and the action

A Lagrangian system on a configuration space M {1} is a smooth function L : Time × TM → ℝ of
time {2} and of the positions and velocities, depending on first derivatives only. [1] A smooth
variation of a curve γ on [t₀, t₁] is a smooth family of curves starting at γ and fixing γ(t₀)
and γ(t₁). [2] The action of γ is ∫ L(t, γ, γ̇) dt over [t₀, t₁], and γ is a critical point of
the action when it is smooth and every variation has zero first variation of the action {3}.
[3] On a normed space, the action is the integral of L(t, q, q̇) along the coordinate curve. [4]

### Equations of motion

On a normed space, a smooth curve is a critical point of the action over [t₀, t₁] with
t₀ ≠ t₁ if and only if the Euler–Lagrange equations hold. [5] A smooth curve is a critical point
of the action if and only if the Euler–Lagrange equations hold in every chart {4}. [TODO]
Lagrangians L(q, q̇, t) written in generalised coordinates are Lagrangian systems {5}. [TODO]

### Symmetries and conservation laws

Noether's theorem: if an autonomous Lagrangian system admits a one-parameter group of
diffeomorphisms of M, then its Lagrange equations have a first integral {4}. [TODO] The
conservation of momentum and of angular momentum follow from Noether's theorem. [TODO] The energy
of an autonomous Lagrangian system is constant along its motions. [TODO]

### Natural systems

A natural system is one whose Lagrangian is kinetic minus potential energy, the kinetic energy
coming from a Riemannian metric on M. [TODO]

The configuration space {1} of the sliding pendulum {2} is given by two generalized coordinates: the
horizontal position of the support and the angle the string makes with the vertical. [1]

The configuration space of the simple pendulum {3} is a manifold. [2] It maps into physical space
{4}, giving the position of the bob there. [3] A trajectory of the simple pendulum is a curve in its
configuration space, and every lift of the angle to the real line describes one. [4] The Lagrangian
of the simple pendulum is a function of the lifted angle and angular velocity, and along a
differentiable lift it agrees with the constrained Lagrangian of the bob moving in physical space.
[5][6]

content.text:
### Configuration space

The configuration space of the simple pendulum, one of the pendulum configuration spaces {1}, is the
angle of the rod from the downward vertical modulo a full turn, homeomorphic to the circle. [1] That
configuration space is a manifold. [2] Each real angle determines a configuration, with angles
that differ by an integer multiple of 2π representing the same configuration. The map from real
angles to configurations is therefore periodic with period 2π. [3] The configuration space maps
into physical space {2}, sending an angle θ to the position (ℓ sin θ, −ℓ cos θ) of the bob, which
lies at distance ℓ from the pivot. [4]

A trajectory is a time-parametrized curve in the configuration space. An angular lift of a given
trajectory is a real-valued function θ(t) whose value modulo 2π gives the configuration
at each time. Two angular lifts describe the same trajectory precisely when their angles differ
by an integer multiple of 2π at each time. [5] Continuous and smooth angular lifts give rise to
continuous and smooth trajectories, respectively. [6] Mapping a trajectory to physical space
gives the position of the bob, which remains at distance |ℓ| from the pivot. [7]

### Dynamics

The Lagrangian of the simple pendulum is the kinetic energy ½ m ℓ² θ̇² minus the gravitational
potential energy {3}. Its equation of motion m ℓ² θ̈ = −m g ℓ sin θ equates the rate of change of
angular momentum with the gravitational torque, and is equivalent to the scalar form θ̈ + (g/ℓ) sin
θ = 0. [8] The equation of motion holds exactly when the variational gradient of the action
vanishes, and energy is conserved along solutions. [9] The Hamiltonian formulation {4} is
equivalent: the Newtonian, scalar, Hamiltonian and variational formulations agree. [10]

The hanging and the inverted positions are equilibria and solve the equation of motion. The
separatrix energy 2 m g ℓ divides the motions: below it the pendulum never reaches the inverted
position, and above it the angular velocity never vanishes. [11] Shifting the angle by a whole number
of turns leaves the lifted dynamics unchanged. [12] The solution with a given initial angle and
angular velocity is unique, the solutions are symmetric under time reversal, and a pendulum released
from rest swings symmetrically in time. [13] For any initial angle and angular velocity there is a
curve with that initial data which satisfies the equation of motion within ε of the initial instant.
[14]

### Small oscillations and the period

In the small-angle limit {5} the pendulum is a harmonic oscillator of mass m ℓ² and spring constant
m g ℓ: the linearized equation of motion is the oscillator's, its motions exist and are unique, and
the period is 2π√(ℓ/g). [15] The full and the linearized dynamics are related by the cubic bound
m g ℓ |θ|³/6 on the error in the torque, and the difference of the variational gradients of the two
actions is the difference of the torque and the linearized force. [16]

The period of a libration of amplitude θ₀ is 4√(ℓ/g) K(sin²(θ₀/2)) {6}. This formula equals
2π√(ℓ/g) at zero amplitude, tends to the small-angle period as the amplitude goes to zero, increases
with the amplitude on [0, π), and is bounded below by the small-angle period and above by the
small-angle period divided by cos(θ₀/2). [17] It is the period of the solution released from rest
at amplitude θ₀, for amplitudes strictly between zero and the inverted position. [TODO]

### Mass distribution and inertia

A rigid body {1} is specified by its mass distribution, a linear functional on the smooth functions
on space {2}. [1] That functional is continuous. [TODO] The total mass of a rigid body is its
mass distribution applied to the constant function one. [2] The centre of mass is the mass-weighted
average of the coordinate functions. [3] The inertia tensor of a rigid body, I_ij = ∫ (δ_ij |x|² −
x_i x_j) dm, is built from the second moments of its mass distribution about the origin. [4] It is
symmetric. [5] The inertia tensor about an arbitrary point takes its moments about that point, and
the parallel-axis theorem expresses it as the inertia tensor about the centre of mass plus that of a
point mass at the centre of mass. [6]

The solid sphere of mass m and radius R > 0, with uniform density on the closed ball about the
origin, is a rigid body whose total mass is m and whose centre of mass is the origin. [7] In three
dimensions its inertia tensor about its centre is (2/5) m R² times the identity. [11][TODO]

### Motion

The angular velocity of a rotating rigid body is the skew-symmetric tensor Ω = Ṙ Rᵀ built from its
orientation R, and in three dimensions it is the vector dual to that tensor under the hat map. [8]
The velocity of the centre of mass is the time derivative of the centre-of-mass trajectory. [9] The
rotational kinetic energy at angular velocity ω is ½ ω · (I ω), and the total kinetic energy of a
moving body is half the mass integral of the squared speed of its points. [10] The orientation of a
rigid body is described by Euler angles. [TODO]

content.text:
### Geometry and the FLRW model

The constant-time slices have one of three spatial geometries, spherical, flat or saddle, with
metric profile giving the transverse radius k sin(r/k), r, or k sinh(r/k) in the three
cases. [1] The flat geometry is the large-radius limit of the curved ones: the profiles of the
spherical and saddle geometries tend to the flat profile as the curvature radius tends to
infinity. [2]

An FLRW model is a scale factor, positive and twice differentiable on an open interval of cosmic
time {1}, together with a spatial geometry. [3] The spatial geometry supplies the curvature
parameter of the Friedmann equations, positive for the spherical geometry, zero for the flat one
and negative for the saddle one. [3] (For the Robertson–Walker metric see Weinberg {2} and
Baumann {3}.)

### The Friedmann equations

The first-order Friedmann equation (∂ₜ a / a)² = (8πG/3) ρ − k c² / a² + Λ c² / 3 relates a
scale factor and an energy density, with the curvature parameter explicit; the second-order
Friedmann equation ∂ₜ ∂ₜ a / a = −(4πG/3) (ρ + 3 p / c²) + Λ c² / 3 involves a pressure as well
and has no curvature term. The cosmological constant, Newton's constant and the speed of light
appear explicitly in both; the speed of light is positive by construction, so no result needs a
hypothesis on it. [8]

A cosmic fluid is an energy density and a pressure, each a function of cosmic time; the empty
fluid has zero density and pressure. [4] A model filled with a fluid solves the Friedmann equations
when both hold on the interval of the model, the curvature parameter being read off the spatial
geometry. [4] Every such solution satisfies the continuity equation [5] and the closure relation
of the density parameters. [6] The de Sitter model at all times, and the Milne model after its
Big Bang, each filled with the empty fluid, solve the Friedmann equations. [17][7] The flat
power-law models, filled with their fluid, solve the Friedmann equations on t > 0 for the matching
equation of state. [25] The radiation-dominated and Einstein–de Sitter models are the cases n = 1/2
and n = 2/3, and after their Big Bang they too solve the Friedmann equations. [26][27]

### Hubble and deceleration parameters

The Hubble parameter H = ∂ₜ a / a is a function of the scale factor and cosmic time, and is
nonzero wherever the scale factor and its derivative both are. [9] The deceleration parameter is
q = −(∂ₜ ∂ₜ a) a / (∂ₜ a)². The derivative ∂ₜ H obeys the quotient-rule formula, q equals
−(1 + (∂ₜ H) / H²) and ∂ₜ H equals −H² (1 + q), and ∂ₜ H < 0 holds exactly when q > −1, both
pointwise and in existential form. [10]

### Matter content

The continuity equation ∂ₜ ρ + 3 H (ρ + P/c²) = 0 of the cosmic fluid holds at an instant
whenever the first-order Friedmann equation holds throughout a neighbourhood of that instant
together with the second-order equation; conversely, the second-order equation follows from the
first-order equation and the continuity equation wherever the scale factor is changing. [11]
(See Dodelson and Schmidt {4} for the smooth, expanding universe.)

Under the barotropic equation of state P = w ρ c², the continuity equation implies the density
scaling law ρ t = ρ t₀ (a t / a t₀)^(−3(1+w)), and conversely; dust, radiation and vacuum energy
are special cases. [12] The cosmological constant is itself a fluid, with density
ρ_Λ = Λ c² / (8πG) and pressure p_Λ = −ρ_Λ c², and folding it into the cosmic fluid gives the
fluid with density ρ + ρ_Λ and pressure p + p_Λ. [18] Each Friedmann equation with a cosmological
constant is equivalent to the same equation without one for the combined fluid, and that
pressure is the w = −1 barotropic pressure of that density. [13] Hence a solution of the Friedmann
equations with Λ is a solution without Λ for the combined fluid. [19]

### Density parameters, the standard model and the age

The critical density of an FLRW model is ρ_cr = 3 H² / (8πG), and the density parameters are
Ω = ρ / ρ_cr for a cosmic fluid in the model, Ω_K = −k c² / (H² a²), k being the curvature parameter
of its spatial geometry, and Ω_Λ = Λ c² / (3 H²), the density parameter of the cosmological constant
as a fluid; folding the cosmological constant into the fluid adds Ω_Λ to its density parameter. [14]
For a solution of the Friedmann equations, the first-order equation is the closure relation
Ω + Ω_Λ + Ω_K = 1 at the times of its interval at which H ≠ 0. [6]

The standard cosmological model has reduced Hubble function
E(x)² = Ω_Λ + Ω_m x⁻³ + Ω_r x⁻⁴ + Ω_K x⁻², with H = H₀ E(a / a₀) for a solution of the Friedmann
equations whose cosmic fluid is made of matter and radiation obeying their scaling laws between two
times of its interval, and with radiation–matter and matter–Λ equality scale factors. [15] The age
of the universe is t₀ = H₀⁻¹ ∫₀¹ dx / (x E(x)). [16]

### Energy conditions and acceleration

The null, weak, strong and dominant energy conditions of the cosmic fluid are defined, with the
implications between them: the dominant condition implies the weak one, and the weak and strong
conditions each imply the null one. [20] On the interval of a solution of the Friedmann equations
the universe accelerates, 0 < ∂ₜ ∂ₜ a, exactly when ρ + 3 p / c² < 0, without and with Λ; and the
deceleration parameter is q = ½ Σ_i Ω_i (1 + 3 w_i) in terms of the density parameters of
barotropic components, with its ΛCDM special case. [21]

### Eternal expansion and the Big Bang

An FLRW model that decelerates on its interval and is expanding at t₀ lies below its tangent line
at t₀, so it cannot be defined earlier than t₀ − 1 / H(t₀) and its interval is bounded below. [22]
On the interval of a solution, for a spatial geometry of non-positive curvature, 0 ≤ Λ and positive
density, the expansion never stops; with 0 ≤ ρ, 0 ≤ p and Λ = 0 the solution decelerates, so it
has a Big Bang in the finite past. [23] The de Sitter model, by contrast, is defined at all times.
[24]

### Distances, redshift and horizons

The distances are defined for an FLRW model, at the times of its interval. The comoving distance
of a source emitting at t and observed at t₀ is χ = c ∫ dτ / a from t to t₀, so that
∂ₜ χ = −c / a. The redshift is 1 + z = a(t₀) / a(t), with ∂ₜ z = −(1 + z) H, and ∂ₜ a = a H;
combining the two, ∂ₜ χ = (c / (a(t₀) H)) ∂ₜ z, the change of variables dχ = c dz / H for
a(t₀) = 1. The proper distance D = a χ obeys the Hubble–Lemaître law ∂ₜ D = H D, and the recession
velocity ∂ₜ D equals c exactly at the Hubble radius R_H = c / H. [28] The transverse comoving
distance r(χ) is the profile of the spatial geometry of the model. With K its curvature parameter
and curvature radius 1 / √|K|, it is (1 / √K) sin(√K χ), χ or (1 / √(−K)) sinh(√(−K) χ) for
positive, zero or negative K. The particle and event horizons at t integrate c / a over the times
of the interval before and after t, and the particle horizon of the Einstein–de Sitter model is
3 c t₀^(2/3) t^(1/3). [29]

The energy of a photon scales as E ∝ 1 / a along its null geodesic, and the comoving distance is
the integral χ = c ∫ dz / H(z) in the redshift for a(t₀) = 1. [TODO]

references.3: D. Baumann, *Cosmology*, Cambridge University Press (2022), Chapter 2.

### The potential

An electromagnetic potential is a map from spacetime {1} to contravariant Lorentz vectors {2}; it is
determined by its values, and potentials add, negate, subtract and scale by reals pointwise. [1] A
distributional electromagnetic potential is a tempered distribution on spacetime valued in Lorentz
vectors, and it arises from distributional scalar and vector potentials. [2]

A potential arises from a scalar potential, from a vector potential, and from a pair of
non-relativistic potentials {3}, each with a static variant, and the potential of a pair is the sum
of the potentials of its two members. [3] A connection on a U(1)-gauge bundle determines a
potential. [TODO]

### Fields and Lagrangian

The electric field is determined by the potential, both for functions [4] and for
distributions. [5] The magnetic field is determined by the potential as a vector field and as an
antisymmetric matrix field for functions [6], and as an antisymmetric matrix field for
distributions. [7] The field-strength term of the Lagrangian is built from the potential, with
its gradient, for functions [8], and its gradient exists for distributions too. [9] The
electromagnetic Lagrangian is built from the potential, together with the coupling to a free
current, and both have gradients for functions [10] and for distributions. [11]

references.3: J. D. Jackson, *Classical Electrodynamics*, 3rd ed., Sections 6.2-6.3, on vector and scalar potentials and gauge transformations.

A fluid {1} is the spatial distribution of its velocity, density and pressure, as fields over space
{2} and time {3}; a fluid flow carries the density and the velocity, while the pressure enters
separately through the stress laws. [1][TODO] The flow out of a volume is the flux of fluid
through the boundary of a spatial region. [TODO]

The mass flux density is the momentum density ρ u, the product of the density and the velocity,
whose divergence enters the continuity equation; the convective momentum flux is ρ u ⊗ u. [2] The
equation of continuity, ∂ₜρ + ∇ · (ρ u) = 0, expresses the local conservation of mass, in a
pointwise classical form, through its residual, and in a smooth form that implies the classical one.
[3]

An ideal, inviscid fluid has Cauchy stress −p I, whose divergence is −∇p. [5] Euler's equation is
the equation of motion of an ideal fluid: continuity, Cauchy momentum balance and inviscid stress,
with the conservative and convective forms equivalent for differentiable fields. [4] Bernoulli's
equation states that the Bernoulli function ½ |u|² + h + Φ, with h the specific enthalpy and Φ the
potential of the body force, is spatially constant, locally that its spatial gradient vanishes. [6]

The entropy flux density is ρ s u, with s the specific entropy. [TODO] The energy flux of a fluid
is ρ u (½ |u|² + h). [TODO]

### The lattice and its geometry

The periodic hypercubic lattice in dimension d has L sites per direction and spacing a > 0,
with a finite set of sites and a unit vector in each lattice direction. [TODO]
Nearest-neighbour sites are joined by oriented links, each with a reversed link, and the
elementary squares are oriented plaquettes, whose boundary is a closed loop of four
links. [TODO]

A function on the sites has forward and backward lattice derivatives and a lattice Laplacian;
summation by parts relates them, and for smooth functions they reduce to the continuum
derivatives as the spacing goes to zero. [TODO] The lattice Fourier transform on the periodic
lattice, over the Brillouin zone of lattice momenta, diagonalizes the lattice Laplacian with
eigenvalues (4/a²) Σ_μ sin²(a p_μ / 2). [TODO]

### Scalar fields

A real scalar field configuration is a function from sites to the reals, and the lattice quartic
action is the sum over sites of a^d times the kinetic term, the mass term and the quartic
interaction. [TODO] The Euclidean lattice measure is the product of Lebesgue measures over
sites weighted by the exponential of minus the action, and its partition function is finite and
strictly positive when the coupling is positive, or when it vanishes and the squared mass is
positive. [TODO] Normalizing gives a probability measure on field configurations whose
moments are the n-point Schwinger functions, invariant under lattice translations and the
lattice symmetry group. [TODO] The free lattice scalar field is the centred Gaussian measure
whose covariance inverts the massive Laplacian, with the lattice propagator in momentum
space. [TODO]

### Gauge fields

A link variable assigns an element of a compact gauge group {1} to each oriented link, the reversed
link carrying the inverse; gauge transformations act on link variables by conjugation between the
endpoints, and the plaquette variable is the ordered product of link variables around a
plaquette. [TODO] The Wilson action of a matrix gauge group is invariant under lattice gauge
transformations. [TODO] The lattice gauge-theory measure is the product of Haar measures over
links weighted by the exponential of minus the Wilson action, with a finite, strictly positive
partition function on a finite lattice. [TODO] A site-valued matter field couples to the link
variables gauge-covariantly through the covariant lattice derivative, and the resulting matter
action is gauge invariant. [TODO]

The Wilson loop of a closed lattice path is invariant under lattice gauge transformations, and
the area-law and perimeter-law behaviours of its expectation value are criteria for
confinement. [TODO] By Elitzur's theorem, on a finite lattice the expectation value of an
observable that is not gauge invariant equals that of its gauge-averaged part, so a local gauge
symmetry cannot be spontaneously broken. [TODO] In the strong-coupling regime of lattice
gauge theory with a compact gauge group, Wilson loops obey the area law. [TODO]

### Structural results and the continuum limit

The lattice measure is reflection positive in the sense of Osterwalder and Schrader, for the
scalar field and for the Wilson action, with respect to reflections in lattice
hyperplanes. [TODO] The transfer matrix is a positive operator on the Hilbert space of
time-slice configurations; it determines the lattice Hamiltonian, and the exponential decay rate
of the two-point function in Euclidean time is the spectral gap. [TODO] For a smooth
continuum gauge field, with link variables given by parallel transport along the links, the
Wilson action converges to the Yang–Mills action as the spacing goes to zero, with corrections of
second order in the spacing. [TODO]

### Fermions

Naive lattice fermions suffer the doubling problem, one continuum species for each corner of the
Brillouin zone, and Wilson fermions remove the doublers at the cost of explicitly breaking chiral
symmetry. [TODO] By the Nielsen–Ninomiya theorem, a local, translation-invariant, hermitian
lattice fermion action with exact chiral symmetry has equal numbers of left- and right-handed
species. [TODO]

### Configurations and the gauge action

A configuration of the two Higgs doublet model is a pair of Higgs vectors {1}. [1] The global gauge
group of the Standard Model acts on such a pair. [2] Configurations form a real vector
space. [TODO] A group of order two acts by swapping the two Higgs vectors. [TODO]

### Gram matrix and Gram vector

The Gram matrix of a configuration is self-adjoint, with nonnegative determinant and
trace. [3] Two configurations lie in the same gauge orbit exactly when they have the same Gram
matrix. [4] Conversely, every self-adjoint matrix with nonnegative determinant and trace is the
Gram matrix of some configuration. [5] Expanding the Gram matrix in the basis of Pauli matrices
gives the Gram vector, which likewise characterizes gauge orbits and is surjective onto the
vectors satisfying the corresponding constraints. [6]

### The potential and its stability

The potential is parameterized following the convention of {2}; these parameters are related to the
reparameterization adapted to the Gram vector used in {3}. [7] The potential of the two Higgs
doublets is the sum of a mass term and a quartic term. [8] The potential, and each of its two terms,
is invariant under the global gauge group. [9] Each of them is a function of the Gram vector
alone. [10]

The potential is stable when it is bounded below. Stability is characterized through the reduced
mass and quartic terms, functions on the unit ball of normalized Gram-vector directions: the reduced
quartic term is nonnegative there and, wherever the reduced mass term is negative, its square is
bounded by a fixed multiple of the reduced quartic term. [11] Strong stability, the positivity of
the reduced quartic term, implies stability. [12] The stability arguments follow, in part, those of
{3}, but one of its steps is false: there is an unstable potential whose reduced quartic term is
nonnegative, and whose reduced mass term is nonnegative wherever the reduced quartic term
vanishes. [13]

references.3: arXiv:hep-ph/0605184, https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0605184

### The full gauge group

The full gauge group is SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1); it projects onto each of its three factors, and an
element is determined by its three projections. [1] Its star operation commutes with the three
projections. [2] Sending a phase a to the diagonal matrix diag(a, ā) gives a homomorphism from
U(1) into SU(2); an element of SU(2) with vanishing upper-right entry is of this form. The electromagnetic U(1), generated by Q = T₃ + Y, embeds in the gauge group as u ↦ (1, diag(u³, ū³), u), fixing a nonzero Higgs vacuum of the form (0, v). Its projections onto SU(3), SU(2) and U(1) are computed explicitly. [3]
The unbroken gauge group SU(3) × U(1)_EM, color together with electromagnetism, is a group in its
own right, included in the gauge group as (h, u) ↦ (h, diag(u³, ū³), u), with its projections
computed explicitly. [13]
The gauge groups are Lie groups. [11][TODO]
The gauge bundle over spacetime and its global sections, the gauge transformations, are built
from the full gauge group. [12][TODO]

### Central subgroups and quotients

The sixth roots of unity embed in the gauge group as a central subgroup, built factor by factor;
membership in it has an explicit description, and it is normal. [4] The quotient of the gauge
group by that subgroup is a group, with its projection from the full group. [5] The second roots
of unity form a central subgroup contained in the sixth-roots subgroup, with its own
quotient. [6] So do the third roots of unity. [7] The center of the full gauge group is
characterized exactly, and not merely shown to contain these subgroups. [TODO]

The choice of quotient, which the physics known so far does not settle {1}, is itself a parameter,
ranging over the sixth, second and third roots of unity and the trivial quotient; for each choice
there is a gauge group and a central subgroup, normal and contained in the sixth-roots subgroup. [8]
A single quotient map out of the full gauge group serves every choice: it is computed on each
central embedding, and its kernel is exactly the chosen subgroup. [9]

### Higgs-sector representations and beyond

On the two-dimensional complex space of the Higgs sector {2}, U(1) acts by a representation and
SU(2) by its fundamental action, and the two commute. [10] The fermionic content of the Standard
Model, together with its representations of the gauge group, forms a single structure. [TODO]

content.text:
### Pointwise Higgs values

The pointwise Higgs values form a two-dimensional complex Euclidean space. [1] They carry an
orthonormal basis, and a real mass scale determines a Higgs vector with the expected norm. [2]
They correspond to four real scalar coordinates. [3]

The global Standard Model gauge group {1} acts on them through a representation, given explicitly as
a U(1) phase times an SU(2) matrix and compatible with the group law. [4] That representation
preserves inner products and norms. [5] Two Higgs vectors lie in the same gauge orbit exactly when
they have the same norm. The electromagnetic U(1) leaves the Higgs vacuum (0, v) invariant, and
one of its elements removes the phase of the first component. [6] The stability group of a Higgs vector is the gauge group it leaves
unbroken: for the vacuum (0, √a) it is SU(3) × U(1)_EM, for any other nonzero Higgs vector it is
a conjugate of this, and the subgroup fixing every Higgs vector is SU(3) × ℤ₆. [7] Pairs of Higgs vectors, with this
gauge action, are the configurations of the two Higgs doublet model {2}.

### The Higgs bundle and Higgs fields

The Higgs bundle over spacetime {3} is a smooth vector bundle, currently the trivial bundle with
fibre the pointwise Higgs values. [8] It is the bundle associated to the gauge group, rather than
the trivial one. [TODO]

Higgs fields are smooth sections of the Higgs bundle; each has an underlying map to pointwise
Higgs values, and every Higgs vector gives a constant field. [9] The components of a Higgs field
are smooth, real and imaginary parts alike. [10] The pointwise inner product of two Higgs fields
has an explicit expansion, is conjugate symmetric and additive, and is smooth. [11] The pointwise
norm squared of a Higgs field is the real part of its inner product with itself, is nonnegative,
and is smooth. [12]

Gauge transformations act on Higgs fields pointwise; two Higgs fields lie in the same orbit
exactly when their pointwise norms squared agree, and every smooth nonnegative function on
spacetime is the norm squared of some Higgs field. [13][TODO] Since the gauge group preserves
inner products and norms of Higgs vectors, the pointwise inner product and norm squared of Higgs
fields are gauge invariant. [5]

### The Higgs potential

The Standard Model Higgs potential {4} has a mass parameter and a quartic coupling, and evaluates
smoothly on a Higgs field; negating both parameters negates the potential, and the potential
vanishes on the zero field; at each spacetime point it is gauge invariant. [14] Completing the
square writes it as a quadratic in the norm squared, whose discriminant is nonnegative and
vanishes exactly in a characterized case. [15]

A bounded-below potential has nonnegative quartic coupling, and a positive quartic coupling makes
it bounded below. [16] The values it attains, its bounds when the discriminant vanishes, and its
minimum for positive and maximum for negative quartic coupling are all determined
explicitly. [16]

### Effective potentials

An effective potential is a function on pointwise Higgs values; when it is gauge invariant it is
constant on gauge orbits and so factors through the norm. [17] An effective potential of bounded
mass dimension is polynomial, splits into homogeneous terms of each mass dimension whose odd terms
vanish when it is invariant, and is then a sum of powers of the norm. [18] Effective potentials
determine potentials on Higgs fields, so that field-level statements follow from pointwise
invariant ones. [TODO] Higgs fields have covariant derivatives and kinetic terms, built from a
gauge connection over spacetime. [TODO]

### Cobordisms and functors

The cobordism category in dimension d has closed oriented (d−1)-manifolds as objects and
oriented cobordisms, taken up to boundary-preserving diffeomorphism, as morphisms, composed by
gluing along a common boundary. [TODO] Disjoint union makes it symmetric monoidal, with the
empty (d−1)-manifold as unit. [TODO] A topological field theory in dimension d is a symmetric
monoidal functor from this category to the modules over a fixed commutative ring. [TODO]
This is the axiomatization of Atiyah {1}, modelled on Segal's definition of conformal field
theory {2}.

### State spaces and partition functions

A closed oriented (d−1)-manifold has a state space, which is finitely generated, and finite
dimensional when the ground ring is a field. [TODO] The state space of a disjoint union is
the tensor product of the state spaces, and the empty manifold has the ground ring as its state
space. [TODO] The map of a cobordism cut along a closed (d−1)-manifold is the composite of
the maps of the two pieces. [TODO] A closed oriented d-manifold has a partition function, an
element of the ground ring invariant under orientation-preserving diffeomorphism. [TODO]

Reversing orientation dualizes: the state space of the reversed manifold is dual to the
original, and the pairing between them coming from the cylinder is nondegenerate. [TODO] A
cylinder induces the identity on the state space, so a topological theory has no time evolution
on a fixed spatial slice. [TODO] The partition function of the product of a closed
(d−1)-manifold with a circle is the rank of the state space of that manifold. [TODO]

### Classification in low dimension

In dimension two, topological field theories valued in vector spaces over a field are
equivalent to commutative Frobenius algebras {3}. [TODO] In dimension one, topological field
theories are equivalent to finitely generated projective modules. [TODO] Topological quantum
mechanics is the one-dimensional case on the time manifold {4}, whose world-volume carries an
orientation but no metric (see issue #877 {5}). [TODO] The general classification programme
is that of Lurie {6}.

### Topological gauge theories

The Chern–Simons action of a connection on a principal bundle over a closed oriented
three-manifold is independent of any metric, gauge invariant up to a shift by an integer
multiple of the level, and has the flat connections as its critical points. [TODO] The BF
action in general dimension is independent of any metric, and its field equations say that the
connection is flat and the second field is covariantly constant. [TODO] Wilson-loop
observables of a topological gauge theory are gauge invariant, and their expectation values give
link invariants. [TODO] These are the ideas of Witten {7}. The Dijkgraaf–Witten
theory of a finite gauge group has as partition function the count of principal bundles over
the manifold weighted by a group cocycle. [TODO]

references.2: G. Segal, *The definition of conformal field theory*, in *Differential Geometrical Methods in Theoretical Physics* (1988), 165–171.
references.3: J. Kock, *Frobenius Algebras and 2D Topological Quantum Field Theories*, Cambridge University Press (2003).
references.6: J. Lurie, *On the classification of topological field theories*, Current Developments in Mathematics 2008 (2009), 129–280.
references.7: E. Witten, *Quantum field theory and the Jones polynomial*, Communications in Mathematical Physics 121 (1989), 351–399.

content.text:
The Hilbert space on space {1} with respect to a measure is the space of square-integrable complex
functions modulo equality almost everywhere, and the volume is the default measure. [1] A
function can be read as an element of such a Hilbert space exactly when it is almost everywhere
strongly measurable and square-integrable. [2]

Several subspaces carry the extra regularity that differential operators need. The complex
Schwartz maps on space form a subspace, and a map passes in either direction between a Schwartz
map and the class it represents. [3] The Sobolev spaces are subspaces too. [TODO] The Fourier
transform is a unitary map from the Hilbert space to itself. [4]

Restricting attention to a region of space gives further structure. The functions supported in a
given subset of space form a Hilbert space of their own, with an inclusion into the full space
and a projection onto it. [5] The elements satisfying homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions
on a subset of space form a subspace. [6] So do the elements satisfying homogeneous Neumann
boundary conditions [TODO], and those satisfying homogeneous mixed boundary conditions.
[TODO]

Operators on these spaces come in two families. Any complex function of position gives a
multiplication operator with maximal domain [7], and the position operators are such
multiplication operators. [8] Any complex function of the wavenumber gives a derivative operator
with maximal domain [TODO], and the momentum and momentum-squared operators are such
derivative operators. [TODO] The angular momentum and angular momentum-squared operators act
on the Hilbert space [TODO], as does the reflection through a general hyperplane. [TODO]
The general theory of these operators lives in the operator algebra {2}.

Two Hilbert spaces have a complete tensor product, the completion of their algebraic tensor
product. [1] It is commutative, by a linear isometry equivalence exchanging the factors [2], and
associative, by a linear isometry equivalence rebracketing three factors. [3] On the algebraic
tensor product of three spaces this rebracketing is the algebraic one. [4] Whenever either
factor is finite-dimensional, the complete tensor product is isometrically equivalent to the
algebraic one. [TODO]

The construction extends beyond pairs. An indexed family of Hilbert spaces has a complete tensor
product [TODO], and a single Hilbert space has complete tensor powers. [TODO] A seed Hilbert
space has a Fock space built from its tensor powers. [TODO]

content.text:
### Unbounded operators

An operator on a Hilbert space is a partially defined linear map. It has a dense domain when its
domain is a dense subspace, and it is unbounded, in the technical sense used here, when it is
densely defined and closable. [1] It is symmetric when the inner-product pairing is symmetric on its
domain, which happens exactly when the pairing of each vector with its own image is real. [2]
Symmetry is stable under sums, powers and closures, and a self-adjoint operator is symmetric and
closed. [3] An operator is essentially self-adjoint when its closure is self-adjoint; such an
operator is unbounded, and its closure is its only self-adjoint extension. [4]

The adjoint is antitone and conjugate-linear in non-zero scalars, the sum of two adjoints is a
restriction of the adjoint of the sum, and likewise for compositions; the adjoint of an unbounded
operator is again unbounded, and its second adjoint is its closure. [5] A symmetric densely defined
operator for which T + i and T - i both have the whole space as range is self-adjoint. [6]
Conjugation by a unitary preserves formal adjoints, dense domains and surjectivity of T - z. [7] The
standard examples separating the classes of symmetric, essentially self-adjoint and self-adjoint
operators make the distinction between symmetry and self-adjointness visible. [TODO] These
definitions follow the standard treatments of unbounded operators by Hall {1}, Reed and Simon {2},
and Schmüdgen {3}. The spectrum, the resolvent, the numerical range and spectral measures of these
operators belong to spectral theory {4}.

### Multiplication operators

A complex function on space {5} gives a multiplication operator on the Hilbert space on space {6},
defined on its maximal domain, the vectors whose product with the function is still
square-integrable; for an almost everywhere strongly measurable multiplier the operator is densely
defined. [8] For a bounded multiplier the domain is the whole
space, and for a multiplier of temperate growth it contains the Schwartz maps. [9] The adjoint of a
multiplication operator is multiplication by the conjugate function, so a real multiplier gives a
self-adjoint operator; multiplication operators are closed and unbounded. [10] They behave
predictably under scalar multiples, sums and composition. [11]

### Position and momentum

Each component of the position operator is multiplication by a coordinate, first on Schwartz maps
and then as a partially defined operator on the Hilbert space, where it is densely defined,
self-adjoint and unbounded. [12] Multiplication by a power of the radius, and by its smooth
regularization, supplies the multipliers of central potentials; the product stays square-integrable
under an explicit condition, and the regularized operators converge to the unregularized one. [13]

Each component of the momentum operator is -iℏ∂ᵢ, first on Schwartz maps and then as a partially
defined operator, which is densely defined, symmetric and unbounded on the Schwartz submodule; the
momentum squared acts on the same domain. [14] On the Sobolev space H¹ the momentum operator is
self-adjoint, and not merely symmetric, and likewise the momentum squared on H². [TODO]

### Commutation relations

Position and momentum satisfy the canonical commutation relation [xᵢ, pⱼ] = iℏ δᵢⱼ on Schwartz maps,
and Leibniz rules reduce a commutator of products to commutators of the factors. [15] The position
components commute among themselves, as do the momentum components, and the commutator of a position
component with the momentum squared is 2iℏ pᵢ. [16] A regularized power of the radius commutes with
itself and with each position component, and its commutators with a momentum component and with the
momentum squared are explicit. [17]

### Angular momentum

The components 𝐋ᵢⱼ = xᵢpⱼ - xⱼpᵢ of the angular momentum operator and the scalar 𝐋² act on Schwartz
maps; the components are antisymmetric in the two indices and vanish for a repeated index, and the
one-, two- and three-dimensional cases each have their own description. [18] Position and momentum
transform as vectors under the angular momenta, which close into the Lie algebra of rotations. [19]
The scalar 𝐋² commutes with every angular momentum component, with the momentum squared and with any
regularized power of the radius. [20]

Each angular momentum component acts on the Hilbert space with dense Schwartz domain, agrees almost
everywhere with its action on Schwartz maps, preserves the Schwartz submodule, and is symmetric and
closable. [21] Angular momentum squared acts on the Hilbert space with invariant dense Schwartz
domain, equals half the sum of the squares of the components, and is symmetric and closable. [22] In
three dimensions the right-handed Cartesian components act on the invariant Schwartz domain, satisfy
the Levi-Civita and cyclic commutation relations, and their three squares sum to angular momentum
squared. [23] The ladder operators L± = Lx ± i Ly act on Schwartz maps and on the Hilbert space with
invariant dense Schwartz domain, where [Lz, L±] = ±ℏ L± and [L², L±] = 0. [24]

Angular momentum extends from its Schwartz domain to self-adjoint operators on the Hilbert space,
whose spectra consist of the eigenvalues ℏ² l (l + 1) of the scalar and ℏ m of a chosen component,
with the spherical harmonics as the corresponding eigenfunctions. [TODO]

### Statistics of observables

The expectation value of an observable T in a state ψ is ⟨T⟩ = re ⟪ψ, T ψ⟫, and the centered vector
is T ψ - ⟨T⟩ψ; for a symmetric operator the pairing is already real. [25] The variance is ‖T ψ -
⟨T⟩ψ‖², given for a unit vector and a symmetric operator by the second-order formula ⟨T²⟩ - ⟨T⟩²,
and the standard deviation is its square root; for a unit vector the variance vanishes exactly when
the vector is an eigenvector. [26] A vector is an eigenvector of a partially defined operator when
it is a non-zero element of the domain sent to a multiple of itself. [27] The covariance of two
observables in a state is symmetric and reduces to the variance on a single observable. [28]

The product of the standard deviations of two observables is at least half the size of their
expected commutator, in both the Robertson and the Robertson-Schrödinger forms, stated for both a
centered and a raw commutator identity. [29] In particular position and momentum obey the Heisenberg
uncertainty relation: in any unit state of a common domain the product of their standard deviations
is at least ℏ/2. [TODO]

These are the textbook notions of Sakurai and Napolitano {7}, Griffiths and Schroeter {8}, and
Hall {1}. The uncertainty bounds go back to Robertson {9} and Schrödinger {10}.

references.3: K. Schmüdgen, *Unbounded Self-Adjoint Operators on Hilbert Space*, Springer (2012), Chapters 1 to 3 (closed, symmetric and self-adjoint operators, and examples 1.3 and 3.8 on multiplication operators).

### Resolvent and spectrum

A complex number z lies in the resolvent set of an operator T {1} when T - z has a bounded inverse,
the resolvent; the resolvent set is open, and for a closed operator it is exactly the set of z for
which T - z is a bijection from the domain onto the space. [1] The spectrum is the complement of the
resolvent set; it is closed, and splits into the point, residual and continuous spectra. [2]
Resolvents satisfy the two resolvent identities, relating resolvents at two points and of two
operators. [3] The treatment follows the standard references of Hall {2}, Reed and Simon {3}, and
Schmüdgen {4}.

### Regularity domain and numerical range

A point z is a point of regularity when T - z is bounded below. The regularity domain is open, the
deficiency subspace at z is the orthogonal complement of the range of T - z, and its dimension is
the defect number; for a closable operator it is constant on each connected component of the
regularity domain. [4] The numerical range is the set of values of the pairing of a unit vector with
its image; it is convex by the Toeplitz-Hausdorff theorem, and the exterior of its closure consists
of points of regularity. [5]

### Symmetric operators

The numerical range of a symmetric operator is real, and so is described by its projection to the
real axis. [6] Every point off the real axis is therefore a point of regularity, and the regularity
domain is connected when the operator is bounded above or below. [7] A symmetric operator whose
defect numbers at i and -i both vanish is essentially self-adjoint. [8] The eigenvalues of a
symmetric operator are real. [9]

### Self-adjoint operators

For a self-adjoint operator the resolvent set and the regularity domain coincide, and every complex
number with non-zero imaginary part lies in the resolvent set, with T - z onto. [10] The spectrum of
a self-adjoint operator lies in the real axis and its residual spectrum is empty. [11] Conjugation
by a unitary preserves self-adjointness, so an observable keeps its status under a change of
representation. [12]

### Spectral measures and the spectral theorem

A spectral measure is a vector measure valued in the bounded operators whose values are star
projections and which sends the whole outcome space to the identity. [13] The projections of two
measurable sets compose to the projection of their intersection, disjoint sets give orthogonal
projections, and all of them commute. [14]

Every self-adjoint operator is the integral of the identity against a spectral measure supported on
its spectrum; equivalently, it is unitarily equivalent to multiplication by a real function on an L²
space. [TODO] The spectral theorem yields a functional calculus, and Stone's theorem gives the
unitary time evolution generated by a self-adjoint Hamiltonian. [TODO] The spectrum of a
multiplication operator is the essential range of its multiplier. [TODO]

references.2: B. C. Hall, *Quantum Theory for Mathematicians*, Springer (2013), Chapters 9 and 10 (unbounded self-adjoint operators, the spectral theorem).
references.3: M. Reed and B. Simon, *Methods of Modern Mathematical Physics I. Functional Analysis*, Academic Press (1980), Chapters VII and VIII (the spectral theorem, unbounded operators).
references.4: K. Schmüdgen, *Unbounded Self-Adjoint Operators on Hilbert Space*, Springer (2012), Chapters 1 to 3 (closed, symmetric and self-adjoint operators, defect numbers, the spectrum).

A quantum system consists of a complete complex inner-product space together with a
self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator on it. [1] The trivial, zero-dimensional Hilbert space carries
a unique quantum system, the zero system. [2] Two systems are unitarily equivalent when some
unitary map between their Hilbert spaces carries one Hamiltonian to the other by conjugation, and
unitary equivalence is an equivalence relation on quantum systems. [3] Two quantum systems add,
giving the system on the product of their Hilbert spaces whose Hamiltonian is, schematically, the
sum of theirs. [TODO]

The dynamics of a quantum system is governed by its Hamiltonian. The Schrödinger equation is an
equation for a wavefunction depending on time and valued in the domain of the Hamiltonian.
[TODO] The time evolution operator is a bounded operator on the Hilbert space for each time.
[TODO] The Hamiltonian has energy eigenspaces, eigenvectors and eigenvalues [TODO], and a
system may admit an energy eigenbasis. [TODO] Conjugation with the time evolution operator
moves an operator into and out of the Heisenberg picture. [TODO]

### States

A qubit {1} is labelled by the two-element type indexing its computational basis. [1] Its pure
states are kets of a finite dimensional system: functions on the basis normalized to unit length, with dual
bras, the bra-ket pairing, the normalization condition in both its componentwise and its
inner-product form, the computational basis states and the uniform superposition. [2] The product of
two systems carries product and entangled kets and the maximally entangled state, so that Bell-type
states of a pair of qubits can be written. [6] Two kets that differ by a unit complex number
represent the same physical state, and the quotient by this relation gives states up to a global
phase. [7]

### Gates

The standard single-qubit gates are the three Pauli gates, the Hadamard gate and the two phase
gates, each an element of the unitary group on a qubit. [3] Each squares to a known gate, the three
Pauli gates anticommute, the phase gates commute with the Pauli gate they are built from and with
each other, and conjugation by the Hadamard gate exchanges two of the Pauli gates. [4] A unitary on
an arbitrary register has a controlled version with a qubit as control; it acts as the unitary on
the block where the control is one, the controlled-NOT gate is the controlled Pauli X gate with its
familiar matrix, controlled gates compose as their targets do, and conjugating the control by a
Pauli gate has an explicit effect. [5]

The rotation gates about the three coordinate axes, together with a phase, decompose an arbitrary
single-qubit unitary, and conjugation by a single-qubit unitary is a rotation of the Bloch sphere.
[TODO]

### The Bloch sphere and geometric phase

The Bloch sphere is the unit sphere of three-dimensional Euclidean space, parameterized by a polar
and an azimuthal angle, and the dot product of two of its points is given in terms of those angles.
[8] A geodesic triangle on the Bloch sphere has a solid angle, and three pure states have a
Bargmann invariant, whose phase is invariant under cyclic permutation and negated under reversal of
the order, as an equation of angles, and whose norm is at most one. [9][10] This phase is
the geometric phase of Pancharatnam {2} and Berry {3}.

The Bloch vector of a state of a qubit is the triple of expectation values of the Pauli gates, and
it is a bijection from states onto the closed unit ball of three-dimensional Euclidean space.
[TODO] It restricts to a bijection from pure states up to a global phase onto the Bloch sphere,
so that the angular parameterization presents the pure state with the given polar and azimuthal
angles. [TODO] Every state of a qubit is one half of the identity plus a real combination of the
Pauli gates, and the identity together with the three Pauli gates is a basis of the self-adjoint two
by two complex matrices. [TODO]

### Measurement and distinguishability

Measuring a qubit in the computational basis gives the two outcomes with probabilities, by the Born
rule, equal to the squared norms of the components of the state. [TODO] The fidelity of two
states of a qubit has a closed form in terms of their traces and determinants. [TODO]

### Pairs and registers of qubits

The Bell basis of the states of a pair of qubits is orthonormal, and the standard gates have an
explicit action on it. [TODO] The singlet and triplet states of a pair of qubits split their
state space into an antisymmetric line and a symmetric plane. [TODO] The positive partial
transpose test is complete for a pair of qubits: such a state is separable exactly when its partial
transpose is positive semidefinite. [TODO]

The state space of a register of several qubits is an iterated product, and a single-qubit gate
extends to a gate acting on one component of a register. [TODO] The Hadamard gate, one phase gate
and the controlled-NOT gate generate a dense subgroup of the special unitary group of a register, so
that they are universal for quantum computation. [TODO] Kets on a qubit are the unit vectors of
the finite dimensional Hilbert space of a two-element type. [TODO]

references.1: M. A. Nielsen and I. L. Chuang, *Quantum Computation and Quantum Information*, Chapters 1, 2, 4 and 9.
references.2: S. Pancharatnam, *Generalized theory of interference, and its applications*, Proc. Indian Acad. Sci. A 44, 247 (1956).
references.3: M. V. Berry, *Quantal phase factors accompanying adiabatic changes*, Proc. R. Soc. London A 392, 45 (1984).

### Dirac spinors

A Dirac fermion is a pair consisting of a left-handed Weyl fermion and a dual right-handed Weyl
fermion {1}. [1] Dirac fermions form a complex vector space, with addition and scalar
multiplication acting on the two Weyl components. [2] Decomposing a Dirac fermion into its Weyl
components is a complex linear equivalence. [3] The space has a four-element chiral basis, whose
elements are the basis elements of the two Weyl components. [4] SL(2, ℂ), the double cover of the
Lorentz group {2}, acts on Dirac fermions componentwise on the two Weyl factors. [5] This
representation is equivalent to the product of the representations on the Weyl components. [6]
The two-component treatment of Dirac fermions follows Dreiner, Haber and Martin {3}.

### Gamma endomorphisms and chirality

Clifford multiplication is a real linear map from Lorentz vectors to complex linear
endomorphisms of the Dirac fermions, written in the chiral basis with the library's Pauli-matrix
conventions; on the Lorentz basis it gives the upper-index gamma components γ^μ. [12] For any two
Lorentz vectors v and w, the anticommutator of their Clifford products is 2⟨v, w⟩ times the
identity, where ⟨v, w⟩ is the Minkowski product; the component relations
{γ^μ, γ^ν} = 2η^{μν}, the squares of the γ^μ and the anticommutation of distinct γ^μ follow, in
the signature (+,−,−,−). [13]

The chirality endomorphism γ⁵ has chiral matrix diag(−1,−1,1,1), squares to the identity, and
anticommutes with every gamma endomorphism. [14] The left and right chiral projectors
(1 − γ⁵)/2 and (1 + γ⁵)/2 have the corresponding diagonal matrices, are idempotent and mutually
orthogonal, and sum to the identity. [15] The chiral projectors are Lorentz equivariant.
[TODO]

### The Dirac representation

An algebra equivalence converts endomorphisms of the Dirac fermions into 4 × 4 matrices in the
Dirac representation, with an explicit change-of-coordinates formula from the chiral basis. [16]
Under it the gamma endomorphisms become the gamma matrices γ⁰, γ¹, γ², γ³ of the Dirac
representation, alongside the chirality matrix γ⁵ and the set the gamma matrices form. [7] These
matrices satisfy the Clifford anticommutator against the Minkowski metric in the signature
(+,−,−,−). [8]

The Dirac slash k̸ of a Lorentz vector k is its Clifford multiplication in the Dirac
representation, contracting the lowered coordinates of k with the gamma matrices. [9] It is real
linear in k, and extends to ordered products of slash factors. [9]

The Dirac algebra is the real subalgebra generated by the Dirac representations of the gamma
endomorphisms, and it contains each generator. [10] The Minkowski quadratic form induces an
algebra map from its Clifford algebra onto the Dirac algebra, and this map is surjective. [11]
The sixteen products of the gamma matrices with increasing indices lie in the Dirac algebra and are
linearly independent over ℝ {3}. [17] The Clifford algebra of the Minkowski quadratic form has
dimension 16 over ℝ. [18] The Dirac algebra has dimension 16 as well. [19] The map from the
Clifford algebra is therefore injective, hence an isomorphism of algebras. [20]

### Bilinears and field equations

A Dirac fermion ψ has a Dirac adjoint ψ̄. [TODO] The Dirac bilinears ψ̄Γψ have definite
transformation behaviour under SL(2, ℂ). [TODO] A spinor field on spacetime is subject to the
Dirac equation. [TODO] A Dirac fermion has a charge conjugate, and the Majorana condition
identifies a fermion with its charge conjugate. [TODO]

references.3: H. K. Dreiner, H. E. Haber and S. P. Martin, *Two-component spinor techniques and Feynman rules for quantum field theory and supersymmetry*, Phys. Rept. 494 (2010) 1–196, arXiv:0812.1594, https://arxiv.org/abs/0812.1594 (Dirac fermions are treated on page 197 of the arXiv version).

### The four spinor spaces

A left-handed Weyl spinor ψ_α is an element of a two-dimensional complex vector space. [1] A
right-handed Weyl spinor ψ^{α̇} is likewise an element of a two-dimensional complex vector space.
[2] Each has a dual, ψ^α and ψ_{α̇}, again a complex vector space. [3][4] Each of the four spaces
has a two-element basis, and every spinor expands in it. [5][6][7][8] Each carries a representation
of SL(2, ℂ), the double cover of the restricted Lorentz group {1}, whose matrix in that basis is the
defining matrix, its conjugate, its inverse transpose or its inverse conjugate transpose as
appropriate. [9][10][11][12] Each of these representations is irreducible, and Schur's lemma
holds for it: an endomorphism commuting with the representation is a scalar multiple of the
identity. [23][24][25][26] Weyl fermions are the building blocks of Dirac fermions {2}, and the
two-component formalism follows Dreiner, Haber and Martin {3}.

### Contractions, metrics and units

Each Weyl type pairs invariantly with its dual, giving bilinear maps that are also intertwining
maps of representations. [13] On basis elements these contractions are Kronecker deltas, and
each is symmetric under exchanging its two factors. [14]

The epsilon metrics ε_{αβ}, ε^{αβ}, ε_{α̇β̇} and ε^{α̇β̇} are invariant tensors, intertwining
maps out of the trivial representation, with explicit expansions in the basis. [15] Their
invariance rests on the raw epsilon matrix ε intertwining M ∈ SL(2, ℂ) with its inverse transpose,
Mε = ε(M⁻¹)ᵀ, and the complex conjugate of M with its inverse conjugate transpose. [16]
Contracting a metric with the metric of the dual type over one index gives the unit,
ε_{αβ}ε^{βγ} = δ_α^γ, and likewise for the other types. [17]

The units δ_α^β and δ^{α̇}_{β̇} realize the duality between each type and its dual, and
contracting a unit with a spinor returns that spinor. [18] Each unit is symmetric under exchange
of its two factors. [19]

### Duality and matrices

The dual of the left-handed representation is the representation on the dual left-handed
spinors. [20] The dual of the right-handed representation is the representation on the dual
right-handed spinors, equivariantly for SL(2, ℂ). [22][TODO] Pairwise tensor products of the
Weyl types are 2 × 2 complex matrices, equivariantly for the action of SL(2, ℂ). [21] The
right-handed representation is the complex conjugate of the left-handed one. [TODO]

### Field equations

A massless spinor field obeys the Weyl equation. [TODO] The Majorana condition relates a
left-handed Weyl fermion to a right-handed one. [TODO]

references.3: H. K. Dreiner, H. E. Haber and S. P. Martin, *Two-component spinor techniques and Feynman rules for quantum field theory and supersymmetry*, Phys. Rept. 494 (2010) 1–196, arXiv:0812.1594, https://arxiv.org/abs/0812.1594.

### The group

A Lorentz transformation is a matrix Λ satisfying Λ * dual Λ = 1, where the dual is taken with
respect to the Minkowski matrix. [1] The Lorentz transformations form a group under matrix
multiplication. [2] Equivalently, Λ is Lorentz exactly when dual Λ * Λ = 1, when its transpose
is Lorentz, when −Λ is Lorentz, or when Λᵀ η Λ = η. [6] The Lorentz group embeds as a closed
subgroup of the general linear group, by a closed embedding. [3] It is a Lie group, by Cartan's
closed subgroup theorem. [TODO] It is the symmetry group of Minkowski spacetime {1}, and Lorentz
tensors {2}, Weyl fermions {3} and Dirac fermions {4} are characterized by how they transform under
it. A standard introduction is Jaffe {5}.

### Boosts and rotations

Every boost is a Lorentz transformation. [4] Every rotation of space is a Lorentz
transformation. [5] Every member of the restricted Lorentz group is a boost composed with a
rotation. [10]

### Proper, orthochronous and restricted transformations

A Lorentz transformation is proper when its determinant is 1. [7] It is orthochronous when it
preserves the direction of time, its time-time component being non-negative. [8] The restricted
Lorentz group consists of the transformations that are both proper and orthochronous. [9] The
orthochronous Lorentz transformations are characterized topologically within the Lorentz group.
[TODO]

references.5: A. Jaffe, *Lorentz Transformations, Rotations, and Boosts*, https://cdn.ku.edu.tr/cdn/files/amostafazadeh/phys517_518/phys517_2016f/Handouts/A_Jaffi_Lorentz_Group.pdf

content.text:
### Group and spacetime action

In $d$ spatial dimensions, a Poincaré transformation is a pair $g=(a,\Lambda)$,
where $a$ is a spacetime translation and $\Lambda$ is a Lorentz transformation.
The product and inverse are
$(a,\Lambda)(b,M)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda M)$ and
$(a,\Lambda)^{-1}=(-\Lambda^{-1}a,\Lambda^{-1})$.
The action $g\cdot x=\Lambda x+a$ is a homeomorphism of spacetime. [1]
The Lorentz group is described in {1}.

### Smooth fields

A transformation acts on a field by inverse pullback,
$(g\cdot u)(x)=u(g^{-1}\cdot x)$; the field values have no additional internal
representation action. The identity acts trivially, composition gives a left
group action, and the action of the inverse undoes the transformation. [2]
For fields valued in a normed real vector space, pullback preserves smoothness
and compact support and defines real-linear maps on smooth fields and compactly
supported smooth test fields. The closed support of a transformed smooth field
is the image of its original closed support under $g$. [3]

### Causal order and reflections

A transformation is orthochronous when its Lorentz part preserves the direction
of time. The identity is orthochronous, as are products and inverses of
orthochronous transformations. [4] The point reflection with parameter $p$ acts
as $x\mapsto p-x$, so its centre is $p/2$. It reverses time orientation. [5]

Orthochronous transformations preserve causal order and take causal futures and
pasts to those of the transformed sets. Transformations that are not
orthochronous reverse causal order and exchange causal futures and pasts. [6]
Here the causal hull of a set means the union of its causal future and causal
past. [7] Every Poincaré transformation maps this hull to the causal hull of the
image, whether or not it preserves time orientation. [8]

### Test functions and distributions

Test functions are smooth, compactly supported functions on the whole spacetime,
with values in a normed real vector space. For each fixed transformation, the
pullback above is a continuous real-linear map on the test-function space and
obeys the left group action law. Its closed support is the image of the original
closed support under $g$. [9]

A distribution with values in a normed real vector space $V$ takes real-valued
test functions to $V$. Its transformed value is
$(g\cdot T)(\varphi)=T(g^{-1}\cdot\varphi)$. For fixed $g$, this defines a
continuous real-linear map on distributions; the identity and composition laws
again give a left group action. [10]

If $T$ vanishes on a set $U$, meaning it annihilates every test function whose
closed support lies in $U$, then $g\cdot T$ vanishes on $gU$. [11]
For real-valued distributions, the delta distribution at $p$ transforms to the
delta distribution at $g\cdot p$. [12]
