content.text:
### Tensor species

A tensor species consists of a symmetry group, a type of index colors, a representation and a
basis for each color, an involution sending each color to the dual color it may contract with,
and contraction and unit data satisfying coherence conditions. [1] A species may carry a metric:
an invariant tensor for each color whose contraction against the metric of the dual color is the
unit, this condition forming a class of its own. [2] The conditions defining a species also relate
the metrics to the basis vectors. [TODO]

### Tensors and their components

Given a species and a list of colors, the tensors with those indices form the tensor product of
the color representations over the index set, and the pure tensors are the choices of one vector
for each index. [3] A component label assigns a basis index to each tensor index. [4] A
component label of a single index is a basis index of its color, a label of a concatenated index
list is a pair of labels, and a label drops a contracted pair of indices. [5][6][7] A tensor
corresponds to its components in the component basis, and the tensors with no indices are the
scalars. [3]

### Group action and reindexing

The symmetry group acts on pure tensors and on tensors. [8] Indices permute along a
color-preserving map, equivariantly, functorially and injectively. [8] The maps that count as
reindexings are characterized and are closed under inverse and composition; they include the
index maps used by products, evaluation and contraction. [9]

### Products

The tensor product of two pure tensors, or of two tensors, concatenates their index lists. [10]
It has explicit components in the basis, is equivariant, and is compatible with swapping the
factors, permuting either factor, and rebracketing. [10]

### Contraction

A pair of indices of dual color contracts, on pure tensors and on tensors, deleting the pair from
the index list. [11][12][13] Contraction is equivariant, commutes with permutations, is symmetric
in the contracted pair, and contractions of two different pairs commute. [13] Its components in
the basis are sums over the contracted label. [14] Contracting inside one factor of a product
agrees with contracting the product. [15]

One tensor also contracts against another at an addressed slot, either with the result placed at
the end [16] or with the result placed at the slot. [17] For real Lorentz tensors the
result-to-end contraction has explicit components in the standard basis. [18]

### Units, metrics, raising and lowering

The unit tensor of a color is invariant under the group action, has explicit components, and is
the permuted unit tensor of the dual color. [19] The metric tensor of a color is invariant, and
contracting it against the metric tensor of the dual color gives the unit. [20] The unit tensor
is an identity for contraction at a slot, so raising and then lowering an index is a round
trip. [21] Raising or lowering a named index, by contraction with the metric, is an equivariant
linear equivalence. [22]

### Evaluation

One index of a tensor evaluates at a fixed basis label, on pure tensors and on tensors. [23]
Evaluation has explicit components in the basis, and commutes with permutations, with other
evaluations, with contractions and with products in their right factor. [23] A tensor is the sum
over basis labels of the evaluations of its last index, each tensored with the matching rank-one
basis tensor and permuted back into the last slot. [23] Evaluation also commutes with a product
in its left factor and with contraction in the opposite order, and two evaluations of the same
tensor commute. [TODO]

### Constructing tensors

Tensors arise from single vectors, from elements of a tensor product of two or three carriers,
and from invariant maps. [24] They also arise from integer components in the standard
basis. [25] Complex Lorentz tensors arise from Gaussian-integer components, compatibly with
products, contractions and permutations. [26]

### Index notation

An elaborator turns pen-and-paper index expressions into tensor operations. [27] The design follows
Tooby-Smith {1}. A class carries index notation to any type linearly equivalent to a tensor, with
the induced group action, basis and products. [28]

### Conjugation

A species may carry a conjugation: a second involution on colors together with a conjugation of
tensors, which is involutive and commutes with contraction. [29] A componentwise criterion for a
tensor to equal a permutation of its conjugate expresses reality, and gives the Hermitian
condition on a metric slot. [29] Both Lorentz species carry conjugations, so that reality and
Hermiticity conditions apply to real and complex Lorentz tensors. [TODO]

### Real Lorentz tensors

The real Lorentz tensors form a species over the Lorentz group {2} with an upper and a lower color,
each dual to the other; in it, contraction is a sum of evaluations. [30] Its colors are carried by
the contravariant and covariant modules, with their representations of the Lorentz group and their
standard bases. [31][32] The two modules contract invariantly against each other. [33] The species
has metric maps [34] and unit maps. [35] Its metric tensors have the Minkowski matrix as components
in the standard basis, and raising or lowering an index multiplies components by the Minkowski
matrix. [36] Its unit tensor has explicit components. [37] Pairwise tensor products of the two
modules are square matrices. [38] The metrics and units of this species are intertwining maps of the
vector and covector representations, with no preliminary constructions or auxiliary modules.
[TODO]

### Lorentz vectors and covectors

A Lorentz vector is a function on one time index and d space indices. [39] Lorentz vectors carry
module, norm and inner-product structures, a charted-space structure, a standard basis and
coordinate maps, a time component and a spatial part, and a model with corners under which they
form a manifold. [39] The Lorentz group acts on them by matrix-vector multiplication. [40] They
are tensorial, the induced action on the standard basis being the matrix action. [41] Lorentz
covectors carry the same structures [42], the same kind of representation [43], and a tensorial
instance. [44] Vectors and covectors contract invariantly against each other. [45]

### Minkowski product and causality

The Minkowski product of two Lorentz vectors is symmetric, Lorentz invariant and
nondegenerate. [46] Linear maps have adjoints with respect to it, and a linear map preserves it
exactly when its matrix lies in the Lorentz group. [46]

Each vector has a causal character — timelike, lightlike or spacelike — that is invariant under
Lorentz transformations, and the product determines light cones, causal precedence and causal
diamonds. [47] A vector is spacelike exactly when its Minkowski norm squared is negative. [47] It
is timelike exactly when that norm squared is positive, and then its time component dominates its
spatial part. [48] It is lightlike exactly when that norm squared vanishes, and causal precedence
is reflexive. [49] A Lorentz velocity is a future-directed vector of unit Minkowski norm; its time
component is positive and dominates its spatial part, and the velocities form a path-connected
set. [50]

### Levi-Civita tensor

The rank-four Levi-Civita tensor is a real Lorentz tensor in three spatial dimensions whose
components in the standard basis are the Levi-Civita symbol, and it is antisymmetric under each
adjacent transposition of indices. [51] The Euclidean Levi-Civita symbol satisfies the
epsilon-epsilon contraction identities summed over all four index slots, over the last three,
and over the last two. [52] At the level of tensors, contracting the Levi-Civita tensor with
itself over all four index pairs gives −24, and over the first three gives −6 times the unit
tensor of the lower color. [63][64][37] A Euclidean Levi-Civita tensor carries the
epsilon-epsilon contraction identities as identities between tensors. [TODO]

### Complex Lorentz tensors

The complex Lorentz tensors form a species over SL(2, ℂ) with the left- and right-handed Weyl colors
{3}, their duals, and the two Lorentz vector colors. [53] The vector colors are carried by complex
contravariant and covariant modules with their representations of SL(2, ℂ), which contract
invariantly against each other. [54][55] The metric tensors [56] and unit tensors [57] of each color
have several equivalent forms, including Gaussian-integer components, and the units are symmetric.
[58] Pairwise products of complex Lorentz vectors are square matrices. [59] The full contraction of
an antisymmetric tensor with a symmetric one equals its own negative. [60] The complex Levi-Civita
tensor has Gaussian-integer components. [61]

### From real to complex tensors

A canonical injective semilinear map takes real Lorentz tensors to complex ones, sending colors
and component labels to their complex counterparts. [62] It is equivariant for the complexified
Lorentz group and commutes with permutations, products, contractions and evaluations of
indices. [62]

A Galilean transformation consists of four pieces of data: a rotation, a boost velocity, a
translation of space {1} and a translation of time {2}. [1]
The spatial dimension is arbitrary; nothing is special to three dimensions. [6]

Galilean transformations form a group, with the identity, the composite and the inverse computed
explicitly from the four pieces. [2] This group is a Lie group. [TODO]

The Galilean group acts on time and space together: an element sends a pair of an instant and a
point to the pair obtained by rotating and boosting the point, then translating both. [7]

The Galilean group is assembled from familiar subgroups, each of which includes into it. The
rotations include into the Galilean group, as do the elements of the full orthogonal group. [3]
The space translations include into the Galilean group. [4] The time translations include into
the Galilean group. [5] More generally, the Euclidean group of space, the transformations
combining a rotation and a translation of space, includes into the Galilean group. [8]

### Frames

A reference frame records a time origin, together with an affine origin and a basis of displacements
of space {1} at each time. [1] Its time origin converts a real time coordinate into an instant of
time {2}. [14] A frame can be built from the trajectories of a collection of reference points,
provided those points form an affine basis at every time: one point serves as the origin, and the
displacements from it to the others serve as the basis. [2] The origin and basis of a frame built in
this way are exactly those points and displacements. [TODO]

A frame may induce the same inner product on coordinates at every time, in which case it
conserves its coordinate metric. [3] A frame may also have orthonormal axes at every time; such a
frame conserves its coordinate metric, and typeclass inference knows this. [4]

### Inertial frames

A frame is inertial when its origin moves with constant velocity and its axes are the same at
every time, both measured against the affine structure that space itself supplies. [5] This is a
restriction on the observer rather than on whatever is being observed. An inertial frame's origin
has a definite constant velocity. [6] Over any elapsed time the origin is displaced by that
elapsed time multiplied by this velocity. [TODO] An inertial frame conserves its coordinate
metric, and typeclass inference knows this. [7]

The relative motion of two inertial frames is the boost, rotation and translation carrying one to
the other, and it induces a transformation law on measured components. [TODO] A frame whose
axes are constant and whose origin moves with constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is
itself inertial. [TODO]

### Measured vector quantities

A vector quantity measured by an observer, a relative position, a velocity, an acceleration, a
force, a momentum, is a list of components read off that observer's axes. These components have
a carrier of their own, equivalent to the tuples of coordinates. [8] They add and scale
componentwise, inheriting the additive and scalar structure of their entries, regardless of which
quantity they stand for; the physical dimension, units and transformation law belong to whatever
supplies the quantity. [9] The components carry a topology, a continuous linear equivalence with
coordinate tuples, and finite dimensionality. [11]

Through the frame's basis at a given time, such components name a geometric displacement in
space, as a linear and as a continuous linear map. [10] Lengths and angles are geometric facts
about that displacement rather than about the numbers. For a frame that conserves its coordinate
metric, the components carry a norm and an inner product pulled back through the frame basis from
displacement space, so that a displacement keeps its length and its angles even when the axes are
skew or unequally scaled. [12] In an orthonormal frame these reduce to the familiar Euclidean
formulas: the sum of the squared components gives the squared length, and the sum of the
componentwise products gives the inner product. [13]

The derivative of a trajectory expressed in a frame gives the velocity and acceleration that frame
measures, as the time derivative of the coordinate components. [TODO]

### Points of space and their structure

A point of space is given by its d real coordinates. [1] Space is a type of its own, distinct
from the Euclidean space of the same dimension although closely related to it, a choice discussed
on the Lean Zulip {1}.
Subtracting two points of space gives a vector of Euclidean space. [8] Space is a normed torsor
over Euclidean space of the same dimension. [9]

Space has a choice of origin, the zero of its vector space structure, and a standard
affine-isometry chart onto Euclidean space of the same dimension. [5] Once the origin is taken as
its zero, space is a real vector space. [2] It carries a norm, an inner product and a metric,
making it a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and a metric space. [3][4] It has basis
vectors, one for each coordinate direction, forming an orthonormal basis. [7]

Space is a smooth manifold, charted over Euclidean space of the same dimension through a
homeomorphism with it. [6]

### Dimensions, units and the cross product

Spaces of different dimensions are related: one dimension of space splits off as a real factor,
and one-dimensional space is isometrically the reals. [14][15] A choice of length unit rescales
lengths, and concrete units such as the metre are available. [16]

Three-dimensional Euclidean space carries the cross product. Taking the cross product with a fixed
vector commutes with the time derivative, and the cross product of a vector with another is
orthogonal to it. [17]

### Translations and rotations

Points of space can be translated, and so can distributions on space. [10][11] The group of
rotations acts on space, and that action agrees with multiplying coordinates by the rotation
matrix. [12][13]

### Derivatives and distributions

A function from space into a normed space can be differentiated along a coordinate
direction. [18] A function from space into a manifold is differentiable. [TODO]

A function bounded in the appropriate sense determines a distribution on space; the constant
function and the constant slice are such distributions. [19][20][21][22] A distribution on space
valued in a normed space can be differentiated, giving also its gradient, its divergence and its
curl. [23][24][25][26] A distribution from space into a manifold is differentiable. [TODO]

### Points of space-time

A point of Minkowski space-time is a Lorentz vector {1} of coordinates, for an arbitrary but
fixed choice of units and origin. [1] Space-time maps onto space {2} and onto time {3}, and is
equivalent to their product. [2]

The Lorentz group {4} acts on space-time, and through it
on Schwartz maps and distributions on space-time. [8] A rotation about the coordinate origin acts
on space-time through the Lorentz group and on space through the Euclidean group, and the
spatial projection intertwines these two actions of one and the same special orthogonal
rotation. [3]

### Integration and slicing

Space-time carries the measure-space structure that integration over it uses: a Borel
measurable space with an additive Haar volume measure. [9] An integral over space-time splits
into an integral over space and an integral over time, in either order. [7] A function or a
distribution on space-time can be sliced at a fixed instant. [10]

### Derivatives

A function from space-time into a normed space can be differentiated along a coordinate, and its
derivatives assemble into a tensor. [4] A function from space-time into a manifold can be
differentiated along a coordinate too, giving a tangent vector at its value. [5] A distribution
on space-time valued in a normed space can be differentiated. [6] A distribution from space-time
into a manifold is differentiable. [TODO]

content.text:
### Instants and their structure

An instant of time is a single real number, for an arbitrary but fixed choice of unit and
orientation. [1] Instants form an affine space over the reals: a real number translates an
instant to another instant, and any two instants differ by a real elapsed time. [2] No instant is
canonically zero.

Given the implicit origin, the instant whose real number is zero, time is a real vector space of
dimension one. It has an orthonormal basis and continuous linear and isometric equivalences to the
reals. [3] Instants are ordered, so that one instant comes no later than another. [4] Time carries
a norm, and an inner product making it a one-dimensional real inner-product space. [5] It is a
Borel measurable space whose volume measure is the Haar measure of the basis, and the
identification with the reals preserves that measure. [6] Time carries an action of the
translation group. [TODO]

Time with no structure beyond its orientation is a manifold in its own right, with its topology,
its charted-space and manifold structures, and a diffeomorphism to the reals. [10]

### Derivatives in time

A function from time into a normed space has a time derivative. The derivative is compatible with
scalar multiplication and with quotients, kills constants, and preserves smoothness. Differentiating
a function valued in Euclidean space, or in Lorentz vectors {1}, agrees with differentiating its
components one at a time. [7] The time derivative of a product of square-matrix-valued functions
obeys the product rule, and the time derivative commutes with the transpose. [9]

A function from time into a manifold has a time derivative too, and for a target that is both a
normed space and a manifold the two derivatives agree. [8]

Distributions from time into a normed space are differentiable. [TODO] Distributions from time
into a manifold are differentiable. [TODO]

### Units of time

A choice of time unit is a positive real number. Two units have a ratio, and a unit rescales an
elapsed time. The concrete units run from seconds up to weeks, with the relations between them,
such as the number of seconds in an hour. [11]

A point of Euclidean space-time is a pair of an instant of time {1} and a point of d-dimensional
space {2}. [1] Space-time projects onto its time and its space
factor, continuously and linearly, and each projection moves a pair of points no further apart
than they were. [2]

The Euclidean group of space acts on space-time, each element as an isometry which splits into a
linear part and a translation. [3] That action carries over to the Schwartz maps out of
space-time, where each element acts injectively and surjectively. [4]

Differentiating a function on space-time in time and differentiating it in space commute, and
the time derivative commutes with the curl. [5] A function on space-time whose time derivative
vanishes depends only on the point of space, one whose space derivative vanishes depends only on
the instant, and one with both vanishing is constant. [6]

### Ensembles and their measures

A canonical ensemble {1} is given by its microstates, its energy function, its degrees of freedom,
its phase-space unit and a σ-finite measure; independent ensembles add, a system has several
non-interacting copies, and an ensemble transports along a measurable equivalence. [1] The
temperature enters through the inverse temperature {2}. An ensemble carries an
unnormalized Boltzmann measure and a normalized probability measure, together with pointwise
mathematical and physical probability densities. [2] The mathematical partition function is the
integral of the Boltzmann factor, and the physical one is that divided by the phase-space unit
raised to the degrees of freedom; both are positive. [3]

### Thermodynamic quantities

An ensemble has a mean energy, a mean square energy and an energy variance, [4] and the
variance is the mean square minus the square of the mean. [5] The Helmholtz free energy comes
from the partition function. [6] An ensemble has a differential entropy and an absolute
thermodynamic entropy, [7] and for finitely many microstates the thermodynamic entropy is the
Shannon entropy. [8]

The fundamental thermodynamic identity holds: the free energy is the mean energy less the
temperature times the entropy. [9] The mean energy is minus the derivative of the logarithm of
the partition function with respect to the inverse temperature. [10] The heat capacity is the
derivative of the mean energy with respect to temperature, and whenever the energy variance is
minus the derivative of the mean energy with respect to the inverse temperature, the heat
capacity is the energy variance divided by the Boltzmann constant times the square of the
temperature. [11] For a finite ensemble at positive temperature this fluctuation–dissipation
theorem holds outright. [12] These identities are developed in Tong's lectures {3}.

### Finite ensembles and the two-state system

For systems with finitely many discrete microstates the integral definitions reduce to finite
sums. [13] The two-state ensemble has closed forms for its partition function, its state
probabilities and its mean energy. [14] Its thermodynamic entropy has a closed form. [TODO]
Its Helmholtz free energy has a closed form. [TODO]

references.1: L. D. Landau and E. M. Lifshitz, *Statistical Physics, Part 1*, §31.
references.3: D. Tong, *Lectures on Statistical Physics* (Cambridge), https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/statphys/one.pdf and https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/statphys/two.pdf

content.text:
### Absolute temperature and inverse temperature

An absolute temperature is a nonnegative real in an arbitrary scale that puts absolute zero at zero;
it coerces to the nonnegative reals and to the reals, carries a topology and a zero, and is
determined by its value. [1] This excludes the negative absolute temperatures that a system with a
bounded energy spectrum can carry {1}. A temperature is built from a nonnegative real, or from a
real together with a proof that it is nonnegative. [7] The temperature enters the Gibbs distribution
through its inverse {2}. A temperature has an inverse temperature, formed with the Boltzmann
constant [14], and a temperature is recovered from an inverse temperature. [2] Passing to the inverse
temperature and back is the identity, in both directions. [3] A strictly positive temperature has a
strictly positive inverse temperature. [4] The boundary value zero is paired with itself, which is a
convention of the underlying nonnegative reals rather than a physical statement.

The temperature is a continuous function of the inverse temperature at positive inverse
temperature, and its real coordinate is differentiable on the positive reals. [5] In the limit
of large inverse temperature the temperature is eventually positive and converges to absolute
zero from above, the regime in which a system settles into its lowest energy states. [6] At
positive temperature the inverse temperature has a derivative with respect to the temperature,
and the chain rule converts a derivative in one variable into a derivative in the other. [8]

### Temperature scales

A temperature unit is a choice of scale, carrying a positive scale factor. [9][10] Two
temperature units have a ratio, a nonnegative real, which is positive and behaves reflexively,
symmetrically and multiplicatively along a chain of units. [11] A temperature unit rescales by a
positive real, with the ratios this induces and its composition law. [12] Kelvin is the reference
temperature unit, and the other units, among them the nanokelvin, microkelvin, millikelvin and
the absolute Fahrenheit-sized degree, are obtained from it by rescaling. [13]

The temperature manifold is diffeomorphic to the nonnegative reals, and a temperature unit is a
translationally invariant metric on it. [TODO] A temperature value converts between two
temperature units. [TODO] Degrees Celsius and degrees Fahrenheit, as ordinarily used, are
scales whose zero is offset from absolute zero, and they convert to absolute scales. [TODO]

references.1: N. F. Ramsey, Thermodynamics and statistical mechanics at negative absolute temperatures, *Physical Review* 103 (1956), 20-28.
references.2: L. D. Landau and E. M. Lifshitz, *Statistical Physics, Part 1*, §9 (temperature) and §31 (the Gibbs distribution).

content.text:
### Dimensions

A dimension assigns a rational exponent to each base dimension, and two dimensions with the same
exponents are equal. [1] Dimensions form a commutative group with a rational power operation.
[2] The exponents of a product, of the unit, of an inverse, of a quotient and of a natural power
follow from the exponents of the factors. [3] Each base dimension has its base vector, whose
exponents are one at that base dimension and zero elsewhere. [4] The vocabulary of base
quantity, derived quantity and quantity dimension is that of ISO/IEC 80000-1 {1} and of the
International vocabulary of metrology {2}. The design of this API is discussed on the Lean
Zulip {3}.

A change of base-dimension set is a monoid homomorphism of dimensions, either an injective
embedding of one set into another or a surjective reduction of a richer set onto a coarser one,
so a relabelling that does not preserve products, inverses and rational powers is not
expressible. [5]

### The LTMCT and ISQ base sets

The LTMCT set has five base dimensions, length, time, mass, charge and temperature, whose
initials give the name, each with its exponent projection. [6] A dimension over this set is
built from its five exponents. [7] Each of the five exponents of a product, a unit, an inverse,
a quotient and a natural power follows from those of the factors. [8] The generators L𝓭, T𝓭,
M𝓭, C𝓭 and Θ𝓭 are the base vectors of the five base dimensions. [9]

The International System of Quantities has seven base quantities. [10] In it electric charge is
derived as current times time, with exponent one in current and in time and zero in mass. [11]
Amount of substance and luminous intensity are base dimensions of their own, distinct from the
trivial dimension. [12]

A faithful embedding carries the LTMCT base dimensions into the ISQ set, sending the charge
generator to the derived ISQ charge. [13] A reduction runs the other way, reading electric
current as charge per time and forgetting amount of substance and luminous intensity. [14] The
reduction is a retraction of the embedding, and the composite in the other order is not the
identity. [15]

### Unit choices and the change of unit

A unit choice fixes one unit for each of the five LTMCT base quantities, with the SI choice of
metre, second, kilogram, coulomb and kelvin. [16] The SI unit choice over the five LTMCT base
quantities is computable, its base units being given without axioms. [TODO] A second unit
choice rescales each SI base unit by a distinct prime, which serves to refute dimensional
correctness. [17]

The factor by which a quantity of a given dimension rescales under a change of unit choice is a
monoid homomorphism from dimensions to the positive reals. [18] It is one on the trivial
dimension and on a unit system paired with itself. [19] It is strictly positive and nonzero,
composes along a chain of three unit choices, and inverts when the two choices are swapped. [20]
Scaling by it is injective. [21] The factor is also available as a strictly positive real, that
is as a unit of the non-negative reals, and it is by this that dimension-carrying quantities are
scaled: no change of unit scales by zero, so the positive reals suffice, and taking them lets a
type whose elements are strictly positive carry a dimension at all. [71] This is the classical
law for the change of a quantity under a change of unit {4}.

### Unit systems over a general base set

The change-of-unit law holds once for a general set of base dimensions and specialises to the
LTMCT set and to the ISQ set without being restated. A magnitude layer assigns a positive real
to each base dimension, with nonzero ratios. [26] On it the scaling homomorphism is the product
over the base dimensions of the unit ratio raised to the corresponding exponent, and it is
transitive. [27] A catalogue names a type of admissible units and a magnitude for each base
dimension, and a unit system chooses exactly one unit per base dimension. [28] A unit system
projects onto the magnitude layer. [29] The five-field LTMCT unit choice is equivalent to a unit
system over the LTMCT base dimensions, and its scaling law is the generic product specialised to
that set. [30][31]

Units of electric current, of amount of substance and of luminous intensity are each a positive
magnitude, with a quotient by another unit of the same kind. [32][33] The coherent SI units are
the ampere, the mole and the candela. [34] These unit types carry the same rescaling operation
as the other five, so that a decimal multiple such as the milliampere exists. [37][38] A unit
choice over the seven ISQ base quantities fixes one unit for each, with the coherent SI choice
of metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. [35] Its scaling factor is the
generic product over the ISQ base quantities. [36] The SI base units are those of the SI
Brochure {5}.

### Dimension-carrying and unit-dependent types

A type may carry a dimension, and the stronger notion is a type carrying a dimension on which
the positive reals act. [22] A function from unit choices to a dimension-carrying type has a
dimension when it rescales by the factor of that dimension under every change of unit. [23] The
functions with this property form a subtype carrying a scalar action. [24] For each fixed unit
choice, a value of a dimension-carrying type is equivalent to a quantity given in every unit
system, and reading that quantity back in the same unit choice returns the value. [25]

A unit-dependent type comes with a transformation of its elements under a change of unit, which
composes along a chain of unit choices and is trivial on an unchanged choice. [39] Stronger
versions require that transformation to commute with a scalar action, to be linear, or to be
linear and continuous. [40] The transformation is then an equivalence, a linear map, a linear
equivalence, a continuous linear map or a continuous linear equivalence. [41] The unit choices
themselves and every dimension-carrying type are unit-dependent. [42] Carrying a dimension is
enough for that on its own, whereas compatibility of the transformation with a non-negative
scalar is meaningful only when such a scalar acts, and so is asked for separately. [72] Function
types are unit-dependent, with the transformation acting on the argument, on the value, or on
both. [43]

A quantity or a statement is dimensionally correct when it is unchanged by a change of unit
system; for functions this unfolds into conditions acting on the argument, on the value and on
both. [44] The dimension-preserving product of two dimension-carrying types scales as the
product of their dimensions. [45] The elements of a unit-dependent type that scale according to
a prescribed dimension form a subset which itself carries that dimension. [46]

### Dimension-tagged values

Values of an underlying type may be tagged with a dimension over any set of base dimensions.
[47] The tagged type inherits zero, addition, negation and subtraction, each computed on the
underlying value. [48] It inherits the order relations and the action of the positive reals.
[49] Multiplying or dividing real-valued tagged quantities multiplies or divides the underlying
values and combines the dimensions in the same way. [50] Over the LTMCT base dimensions a tagged
type carries its dimension, and its transformation under a change of unit is scalar
multiplication by the scaling factor. [51] A tagged quantity of trivial dimension is unchanged
by a change of unit. [52] A cast moves a tagged quantity between two tags whose dimensions are
equal, with the equality discharged automatically. [53] A quantity whose elements are strictly
positive is regarded as a dimension-tagged real by recording its magnitude, with the dimension
read off its type so that the two cannot drift apart, and tagging it commutes both with a
rescaling and with a change of unit. [73]

At a fixed numerical unit representation, tagged values form a real module without replacing the
existing additive operations or the action of the nonnegative reals. [68] They also form a
normed space, and explicit coordinate equivalences transport functions and their Fréchet
derivatives. [69] The tagged type inherits further structure from its underlying type:
multiplicative and other non-additive algebraic structure, the rest of the order structure, and
topological structure. [TODO]

### Named quantities

The base quantities themselves are the subject of the APIs for time {6}, space {7} and
temperature {8}, and of the mass and charge modules.
Area has dimension length squared, with the square metre, square foot, square mile, are, hectare
and acre, their values in SI units, and one acre equal to 43560 square feet. [54] Speed has
dimension length over time, with the metre per second, mile per hour, kilometre per hour and
knot, their values in SI units, and the conversions between them. [55] Energy
has dimension mass times length squared over time squared, with the joule, electronvolt, calorie
and kilowatt hour. [56] Pressure has dimension mass over length over time squared, with the
pascal, millimetre of mercury, bar, standard atmosphere, torr and pound per square inch. [57]
Momentum has dimension mass times length over time and takes values in d spatial components:
it is the three-momentum rather than the four-momentum. [58] The mass of a particle is a named
dimension-carrying quantity in the manner of momentum, and so is its velocity in d spatial
dimensions. [TODO]

### Physical constants

A physical constant is not a unit: it is a definite physical quantity, fixed once and for all,
and the number recording it is determined by the unit system in which it is read. It is
therefore recorded as a quantity given in every unit system rather than placed among the units
of the quantity it measures. The speed of light is such a constant. Its type consists of
strictly positive reals, which is why it needs the scaling by a strictly positive factor, and it
carries the dimension of a length over a time; its value in our world is exactly 299792458
metres per second. [74][75] The Boltzmann constant is recorded in the same way, with the dimension
of an energy over a temperature and an exact value in our world. [77] Newton's constant and
Planck's constant are to be recorded in the same way. [TODO] There are units in which the speed
of light and the Boltzmann constant are both one. [76] In Planck units Newton's constant and the
reduced Planck constant are one as well. [TODO]

### Calculus and dimensional correctness

The derivative of a dimensionally correct differentiable function is dimensionally correct, and
the derivative at a rescaled point is the explicitly rescaled derivative. [59] The equation
giving the derivative in a fixed direction as a quantity of the dimension of the target divided
by the dimension of the source is dimensionally correct. [60] A measure on a dimension-carrying
type is unit-dependent, and the integral of a function whose dimension is that of its values
divided by the dimension of the measure has the dimension of the values. [61]

### Examples

A length of 400 metres converts to miles. [62] The relations E = m c^2 and F = m a, stated over
dimension-tagged reals, are dimensionally correct. [63] A speed as distance over time, an
expression of mixed dimension in mass, temperature, current, length and time, and the cosine of
an angular frequency times a time are each dimensionally correct. [64] The relation E = m c is
not dimensionally correct: a change of unit breaks it. [65] The version of E = m c^2 written with
the speed of light in an explicit unit system holds in SI units and, by transport, in every unit
system. [66]

The equality of a length with a speed times a time holds propositionally rather than
definitionally, so the two tagged types are bridged by a cast, and the same comparison works
over a set of base dimensions with no physical unit system, namely bits and symbols. [67]

The harmonic oscillator carries its mass and spring constant with their physical dimensions.
Its potential energy is assembled from dimension-tagged quantities, agrees in coordinates with
the numerical oscillator, and has its derivative from the generic transport of derivatives.
[70]
